title: True False Not Given: The Thames Tunnel
passage: The Thames Tunnel was a tunnel built under the River Thames in London. It was the first subaqueous tunnel ever built and many people were so amazed that they exaggerated their description of it calling it the Eight Wonder of the World at the time it was opened. It was opened in 1843 to pedestrians only and people came from far and wide to see the marvel. The day it was first opened, it attracted five thousand people to enter the tunnel and walk its length of almost 400 metres. The Thames Tunnel was used by people from all classes. Most working class people used it for its functional use of crossing from one side of the river to the other as they went to work each day, while for the middle classes and upper classes, it was a tourist experience. In the age of sail and horse-drawn coaches, people voyaged a long way to visit the tunnel, but this was not enough to make the tunnel a financial success. It had cost over £500,000 to complete which in those days was a considerable amount of money. However, even though it attracted about 2 million people each year, each person only paid a penny to use it. The aim had been for the tunnel to be used by wheeled vehicles to transport cargo so that it could bring in a profit. But this failed and the tunnel eventually became nothing more than a tourist attraction selling souvenirs and a subaqueous pathway connecting either side of the river. However, in 1865, the tunnel became part of the London Underground railway system which continues to be its use today.

questions.text: The Thames Tunnel was the first tunnel ever built under a river.
questions.explanation: "It was the first subaqueous tunnel ever built." The word "subaqueous" means under water, confirming this was the first tunnel built under a river.

questions.text: The Thames Tunnel was the Eighth Wonder of the World.
questions.explanation: The passage says people "exaggerated their description of it calling it the Eight Wonder of the World" — this was a popular exaggeration, not an official designation.

questions.text: People were drawn from all over to see the Thames Tunnel.
questions.explanation: The passage says people "came from far and wide to see the marvel", meaning visitors were drawn from many places.

questions.text: The tunnel was used more by the middle and upper classes.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes how working class and upper/middle classes used the tunnel differently, but gives no information about which class used it more frequently.

questions.text: People were able to travel by sea or land in those days.
questions.explanation: The phrase "in the age of sail and horse-drawn coaches" confirms both sea travel (sail) and land travel (horse-drawn coaches) existed at the time.

questions.text: The aim of the tunnel was to turn a profit as a tourist attraction.
questions.explanation: The passage states the aim "had been for the tunnel to be used by wheeled vehicles to transport cargo so that it could bring in a profit" — the aim was cargo transport, not tourism.

questions.text: Statues of the tunnel could be bought as souvenirs.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions souvenirs were sold, but gives no information about what type (e.g. statues) they were.

questions.text: The tunnel is no longer used as a pedestrian walkway to cross the river.
questions.explanation: In 1865 the tunnel "became part of the London Underground railway system", so it no longer functions as a pedestrian walkway.

title: True False Not Given: Pyramid Building
passage:
The most famous pyramid is the Great Pyramid of Giza which is actually only one of over a hundred surviving pyramids. There is a long-standing question about how the pyramids were built given the lack of technology over 4,000 years ago but scientists are piecing together the puzzle. The blocks which make up the pyramids were hewn from quarries and then transported to the pyramids for construction. This was an incredible feat considering the distance that the raw materials had to travel and their enormous weight. The transportation of the materials was either by river using a boat or by land using a wooden sledge. Given the softness of the ground, the wheel would have been of little use had it been invented at that time. It is believed that the sand in front of the sledge was wet with water in order to facilitate the movement of the sledge and reduce friction. These sledges were pulled manually or sometimes by using beasts of burden depending on the ease at which the sledges could move over the ground. Interestingly, two thousand years after the pyramid building era of the Ancient Egyptians, the Romans moved stones using similar techniques at Baalbek. Once the blocks arrived at the pyramid construction site, it is thought they were moved into place using a ramp and pulley system.

The Old Kingdom period in Ancient Egyptian history is also known as the pyramid building era. The Ancient Egyptians achieved the most remarkable feats of building work which have still not been surpassed, particularly given the primitive technology used to build them. There is nothing remotely mystical or magical about how the pyramids were built as is commonly thought. Further still, while popular belief is that the Great Pyramid was built using slave labour, this theory has since been debunked. The first building made in a pyramid shape is thought to be the Stepped Pyramid which consists of six steps placed on top of each other in a pyramid shape to create the world's first superstructure. The credit to finally achieving a smooth sided pyramid goes to Imhotep, an architect commissioned by King Sneferu. The pyramids were not an instant achievement, but the achievement of trial and error.

questions.text: The controversy over the method used in the construction of the pyramids has been solved by scientists.
questions.explanation: The passage says scientists are currently "piecing together the puzzle", indicating the mystery of construction methods is still being investigated, not already solved.

questions.text: It is possible that Ancient Egyptians could have lubricated paths to aid transportation by sledge.
questions.explanation: The passage states "it is believed that the sand in front of the sledge was wet with water in order to facilitate the movement", confirming water lubrication was possibly used.

questions.text: Sleds were dragged by animals not humans.
questions.explanation: The passage says sleds were "pulled manually or sometimes by using beasts of burden" — both humans and animals pulled them, so "animals not humans" is false.

questions.text: The Romans learned the techniques of moving huge stones from the Ancient Egyptians.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions Romans used similar techniques at Baalbek, but provides no information about whether Romans learned these techniques from the Egyptians.

questions.text: The building work of the Ancient Egyptians is unrivalled.
questions.explanation: The passage states "The Ancient Egyptians achieved the most remarkable feats of building work which have still not been surpassed."

questions.text: Many people believe that magic may have been used by the Ancient Egyptians to build the pyramids.
questions.explanation: The passage says "There is nothing remotely mystical or magical about how the pyramids were built as is commonly thought" — confirming many people believe magic was involved.

questions.text: The Great Pyramid was built using slave labour.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states: "While popular belief is that the Great Pyramid was built using slave labour, this theory has since been debunked."

questions.text: It took more than one attempt to get the construction of the pyramids right.
questions.explanation: The passage says "the pyramids were not an instant achievement, but the achievement of trial and error", meaning multiple attempts were required.

title: True False Not Given: Beethoven
passage:
Composer Ludwig van Beethoven was born on or near December 16, 1770, in Bonn, Germany. He is widely considered the greatest composer of all time. Sometime between the births of his two younger brothers, Beethoven's father began teaching him music with an extraordinary rigour and brutality, which affected him for the rest of his life. On a near daily basis, Beethoven was flogged, locked in the cellar and deprived of sleep for extra hours of practice. He studied the violin and clavier with his father as well as taking additional lessons from organists around town. Beethoven was a prodigiously talented musician from his earliest days and displayed flashes of the creative imagination that would eventually reach farther than any composer's before or since.

In 1804, Beethoven was completing his third symphony, which he at first named "Bonaparte" in honour of Napoleon. However, when later that year Napoleon proclaimed himself Emperor, Beethoven was so disappointed that he renamed his composition "Eroica". This work, his greatest and most original to date, debuted in Vienna in 1805. It was so unlike anything heard before that through weeks of rehearsal, the musicians could not figure out how to play it. At the same time as he was composing these great and immortal works, Beethoven was trying hard to come to terms with a shocking and terrible fact, one that he tried desperately to conceal. He was going deaf. At the turn of the century, Beethoven struggled to make out the words spoken to him in conversation.

Despite his extraordinary output of beautiful music, Beethoven was frequently miserable throughout his adult life. Beethoven died on March 26, 1827, at the age of 56.

questions.text: It is not known exactly when Beethoven was born.
questions.explanation: The passage states he was born "on or near December 16, 1770", showing the exact date is uncertain.

questions.text: Beethoven's father took a forbearing approach to teaching his son music.
questions.explanation: "Forbearing" means patient and tolerant, but the passage describes his father's teaching approach as involving "rigour and brutality" — the opposite of forbearing.

questions.text: Beethoven's father was also a talented musician.
questions.explanation: The passage confirms his father taught him music but provides no information about whether his father was himself a talented musician.

questions.text: Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 was inspired by a famous man.
questions.explanation: The passage says the symphony was dedicated to Napoleon, but provides no information about what originally inspired its creation.

questions.text: Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 premiered just before Napoleon became Emperor.
questions.explanation: The symphony "debuted in Vienna in 1805", which was after Napoleon became Emperor in May 1804 — so it premiered just after, not before.

questions.text: In the early 1800s Beethoven struggled to follow a conversation.
questions.explanation: The passage states "At the turn of the century, Beethoven struggled to make out the words spoken to him in conversation", confirming early communication difficulties.

title: True False Not Given: Spam Messaging
passage:
SPAM, as every user of mobile phones in China is aware to their intense annoyance, is a roaring trade in China. Its delivery-men drive through residential neighbourhoods in "text-messaging cars", with illegal but easy-to-buy gadgetry they use to hijack links between mobile-phone users and nearby communications masts. They then target the numbers they harvest, blasting them with spam text messages before driving away. Mobile-phone users usually see only the wearisome results: another sprinkling of spam messages offering deals on flats, investment advice and dodgy receipts for tax purposes.

Chinese mobile-users get more spam text messages than their counterparts anywhere else in the world. They received slightly more than 300 billion of them in 2013, or close to one a day for each person using a mobile phone. Users in bigger markets like Beijing and Shanghai receive two a day, or more than 700 annually, accounting for perhaps one-fifth to one-third of all texts. Americans, by comparison, received an estimated 4.5 billion junk messages in 2011, or fewer than 20 per mobile-user for the year — out of a total of more than two trillion text messages sent.

questions.text: In China, SPAM text messaging is a successful business.
questions.explanation: The passage says SPAM is "a roaring trade in China" — "roaring trade" means a thriving, successful business.

questions.text: People's phone numbers are collected through the use of technology which cannot be readily bought.
questions.explanation: The passage describes phone number collection through "illegal but easy-to-buy gadgetry", meaning the technology is accessible, contradicting "difficult to obtain".

questions.text: In no other country do people receive more spam texts than in China.
questions.explanation: The passage states "Chinese mobile-users get more spam text messages than their counterparts anywhere else in the world."

questions.text: In 2013, the number of SPAM texts increased considerably to reach at least 300 billion.
questions.explanation: The passage provides 2013 figures but no comparison to previous years, so we cannot determine whether numbers increased to reach that level.

questions.text: The majority of all texts received in Shanghai and Beijing are SPAM.
questions.explanation: The passage says users receive "perhaps one-fifth to one-third" of all texts as spam — this is a minority, not a majority.

questions.text: In 2011, Americans sent more texts than anywhere else in the world.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions American texting statistics but does not compare them to all other countries globally.

title: Multiple Choice: All About Rice
passage: The first rice may have been grown in East and South Asia as long as 15,000 years ago, when people began to settle in river deltas and domesticated wild rice. Today it is grown practically everywhere, except Antarctica! Rice is grown on flooded land and on dry land, in tropical rain forests of Africa and in arid deserts of the Middle East, on coastal plains and on the Himalayan mountains. In the year 2003, the world produced about 589 million tonnes of paddy rice. Most of that (about 534 million tonnes) was grown in Asia. In 2002, it is estimated that rice fields covered almost 1.5 million square km of land. Again, most of those fields are in Asia — around 1.3 million square km.

questions.text: Where is rice grown?
options: mainly on flood lands and coastal plains
questions.explanation: The passage states rice is grown "everywhere, except Antarctica" — this one exception means it is not grown in literally every location on Earth.

questions.text: In 2002, rice fields covered about ______
options: 1.3 million square km of land in China
1.5 million square km of land in the world
questions.explanation: The passage specifies "1.5 million square km of land" globally in 2002, matching option C.

title: Multiple Choice: GM Foods
passage:
Genetically modified food is produced from plants which have had their genes tweaked in the lab. Scientists "cut and paste" a gene from another organism into a plant's DNA to give it a new characteristic. This can be to increase yield or to allow the plant to exist in a more hostile environment than normal. Pro-GM scientists say this means cheaper more plentiful food but opponents argue we do not know the consequences of meddling with nature.

Farmers have modified their crops for thousands of years by crossing similar species. However, modern GM is controversial. Critics say the modified crops could "escape" and cross with wild plants, with unknown consequences. They also argue that more chemicals are used on some GM fields which may have a negative impact on wildlife. And while no study has found GM food to be harmful to humans, opponents say it is too soon to be sure.

A group of biotechnology experts say it is time to loosen Europe's draconian regulations on genetically modified crops. In a report released today they argue that genetically modified crops have been used safely for decades, so no longer need to be automatically treated as unsafe. They also say that genetically modified crops should be reclaimed from multinational companies and treated as a public good.

questions.text: The genetic makeup of GM foods has been ________
questions.explanation: The passage uses "tweaked" to describe the modification process. "Altered" (B) best captures the meaning of genetic modification in standard English.

questions.text: By genetically engineering plants, they are __________
options: not able to exist in difficult conditions
questions.explanation: The passage references "increase yield", which means producing greater quantities of crops, matching option B.

questions.text: One issue with GM plants is the potential to ________
options: cause undetermined consequences by damaging the fauna
infect wild plants with unknown results
questions.explanation: The passage states modified crops could "escape" and "cross with wild plants" — "cross pollinate" (C) accurately describes this reproductive interaction.

questions.text: It is thought by specialists in biotechnology that policies governing GM crops should be _______
questions.explanation: The passage says experts argue to "loosen Europe's draconian regulations" — "loosen" means to relax restrictions, matching option B.

questions.text: GM foods ought to be ________
options: reclaimed for the use of multinational companies
questions.explanation: The passage states GM crops "should be reclaimed from multinational companies and treated as a public good" — this means removing private ownership, matching option C.

title: Reading Practice: About Ants (Diagram Completion + TFNG)
passage:
There are more than 10,000 known species of ants living throughout the world. Ants can be identified by the constriction that looks like a waist between the abdomen, at the end of the body, and the part of the body called the thorax, which is located before the head. Their bodies are covered with a hard armour called the exoskeleton. While the exoskeleton is their defensive weapon, their rear abdominal stinger is their offensive one. Like other insects, they have six legs; each with three joints. Ants have large heads with compound eyes, elbowed antennae, which act as sensors, and powerful pincers, known as mandibles. These pincers are an ant's most useful tool which are used for grabbing things, cutting and are a kind of trap-jaw.

There are three types of adult ants living in the colony: the queen, female ants, and male ants. Queen ants are the largest ants in the colony. They have wings and their purpose is to lay eggs. The queens can live up to 30 years. Depending on the ant species and the nest community size, there may be one or more queens in the colony. The ant life cycle has four stages of development: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The queen lays the eggs, which will hatch into larvae in a couple of days. The helpless larva are fed and groomed by the worker ants until they pass through the pupal stage. In a little more than a week, an adult ant will emerge and the metamorphosis is complete.

questions.text: Body part at the end of the ant's body (diagram label 1)
questions.explanation: The passage describes the abdomen as "the part of the body at the end of the ant but after the narrow waist" — it is the final, rear section of the body.

questions.text: Middle section of the ant's body (diagram label 2)
questions.explanation: The passage identifies the thorax as the middle section of the ant's body, located between the head and the abdomen.

questions.text: Rear defensive feature used for attacking (diagram label 3)
questions.explanation: The passage refers to a rear abdominal stinger as the ant's offensive and defensive feature located at the back of the abdomen.

questions.text: Head feature used for vision (diagram label 4)
questions.explanation: The passage states "Ants have large heads with compound eyes" — compound eyes are the specialised visual organs found on the ant's head.

questions.text: Powerful mouth parts used for grabbing and cutting (diagram label 5)
questions.explanation: The passage describes mandibles as "powerful pincers" used for grabbing and cutting, located near the mouth.

questions.text: The antennae of an ant cannot bend.
questions.explanation: The passage states the antennae are "elbowed", meaning they contain a joint and can bend. Therefore the statement that "antennae cannot bend" is FALSE.

questions.text: Only queen ants have wings.
questions.explanation: The passage states that queen ants have wings, but does not state whether they are the ONLY type of ant to have wings. Since we cannot determine this from the passage, the answer is NOT GIVEN — the key word is "only".

questions.text: Larva undergo metamorphosis in the pupal stage.
questions.explanation: The passage states that metamorphosis happens "during the pupal stage when the larva change into adult ants", confirming the statement is TRUE.

title: Matching Headings: The Greenhouse Effect
passage:
Paragraph A: A greenhouse is a house made entirely of glass: both walls and roof are glass. One of the main purposes of a greenhouse is to grow tomatoes, flowers and other plants that might struggle to grow outside.

Paragraph B: The Earth experiences a similar thing to a greenhouse. Gases in the atmosphere such as carbon dioxide do what the roof of a greenhouse does. During the day, the Sun shines through the atmosphere.

Paragraph C: However, gas molecules, called greenhouse gases, which absorb thermal infrared radiation, are rising and this is what is altering the climate system.

Paragraph D: Many scientists agree that the damage to the Earth's atmosphere and climate is past the point of no return. Josef Werne told Live Science that we have three ways to move forward.

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.explanation: The paragraph actually talked about what it was made of, what it was used for and how it works. The best title would be "The greenhouse" because the paragraph gives a clear overview of it.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.explanation: The answer isn't I because the paragraph actually explains that this natural effect keeps the temperature of Earth stable. The answer is VI which explains how Earth's atmosphere works to keep our planet at a stable temperature.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.explanation: The answer isn't VIII (Effects of carbon dioxide) because the paragraph isn't aimed at explaining carbon dioxide and in fact only mentions it alongside other greenhouse gases. The answer isn't IX (Climates around the world) because although climates are affected around the world, the whole paragraph aim isn't to discuss climates in different countries. The correct answer is III – Global warming.

questions.text: Paragraph D

The correct answer is VII – Our choices.

title: Yes No Not Given: Richard the Lionheart
passage: King Richard I of England is one of the most iconic kings of England, known as the Crusader King and also as Richard the Lionheart. He spent practically all his reign outside England fighting wars in the Middle East and France to the point that England must have seemed like a foreign, distant land to him. It seems strange to us today to consider a King of England so wholly detached from the country that he represented and ruled. To pay for his wars and crusades, he taxed the English so heavily that it caused widespread discontent amongst the populace. While it can be said that he was a peerless warrior in battle, he was a poor King of England. He has often been criticised not only for his neglect of England and the welfare of the common person, but also for squandering the lives of so many of his followers as they followed him into battles far from their homeland. And yet remarkably, many English people still remember him quite fondly as a chivalrous king who was the epitome of a knight with bravery and military skill.

questions.text: King Richard idolised fame.
questions.explanation: The passage shows that Richard probably didn't connect much with the English culture because he spent so much time abroad, but it doesn't give any information about whether he lacked respect or "looked down on" the English culture.

questions.text: While King, Richard never resided in England.
questions.explanation: He spent much of his reign outside England, but not all his reign — so the statement that he "never resided in England" is NO.

questions.text: King Richard looked down on the English culture.
questions.explanation: The passage does not provide any information about Richard's personal attitude toward English culture itself, so this is NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Many English people did not agree with being taxed so much.
questions.explanation: The passage shows the population of England showed "widespread discontent" with the heavy taxes. "Widespread" means many thought this, but not all — so YES, many did not agree with the heavy taxation.

questions.text: He was a fighter beyond compare.
questions.explanation: "Peerless" in the passage means beyond compare — there were no peers who were his equal as a fighter, confirming the statement is YES.

questions.text: The people who followed him into battle were common people from England.
questions.explanation: The passage shows King Richard did not care about the welfare of the common people, but we do not know precisely who his followers in battle were. NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: King Richard did not place much consideration on the value of a human life.
questions.explanation: The passage states he was "squandering the lives of so many of his followers" — "squandering" means to waste, confirming he placed little value on human life. The answer is YES.

questions.text: King Richard is considered by all English people as a courageous knight.
questions.explanation: The challenge with this question is the word "all" in the question versus "many" in the passage. Not all English people — only many — considered him a courageous knight, making the answer NO.

title: Sentence Completion: Neighbourhood Badgers
passage: Badgers in gardens can be a delight. A nightly treat that householders all over the country look forward to. But for some, they are at the very least unwelcome visitors, threatening cherished pristine lawns and carefully cultivated vegetables because badgers find food where they can and have little respect for people's efforts in gardening. Often unseen and unheard, they wander quietly into gardens at night, feeding on the earthworms, grubs, snails and slugs they find in lawns and borders before moving on. In their wake, they leave only the slightest clues, an odd small snuffle hole here and there, showing where they obviously sought out their nightly treat. If it is suspected there is a badger sett in a garden, expert advice should be sought. It's easy to know if there is one by the many holes you'll find which tunnel down to various living chambers in their underground sett. People should not try to interfere with them in this situation, as it is against the law. Badgers will not cause people any harm or pass on diseases so they should be left to live quietly in their residence but their presence should be reported to an expert who can rehome them if necessary. There are some fascinating facts about badgers. Badgers are extremely clean animals and do not take food into their setts preferring to eat out in the open and retain a clean living area underground. They are remarkably suited to their purpose of digging, having powerful claws and limbs. American badgers even have a third eyelid that keeps out grains of sand and soil. Interestingly, the idiom we know as "to badger someone" comes from an old sport of Badger Baiting rather than their actual character. The idiom actually means to tell someone to do something or to question them again and again — incessantly without let up.

questions.text: While badgers are seen as a delight by some people, others see them as ________.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts those who see badgers as "a delight" with those who see them as "unwelcome visitors". Both words are needed as they appear together in the passage.

questions.text: A ________ is a sure way to know a badger has visited a garden.
questions.explanation: A "snuffle hole" is a specific type of hole made by badgers searching for food using their nose/mouth. The word "snuffle" cannot be omitted because it describes the particular nature of the hole, not just any hole — "snuffle" denotes both the hole's origin and its type.

questions.text: It is best not to ________ with badgers if they have made a home in your garden.
questions.explanation: The passage states directly: "People should not try to interfere with them in this situation, as it is against the law."

questions.text: Badgers do not transmit ________ to humans.
questions.explanation: The passage reads: "Badgers will not cause people any harm or pass on diseases so they should be left to live quietly." The answer is "diseases".

questions.text: Badgers are built for digging and some also have a protective ________.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions "American badgers even have a third eyelid that keeps out grains of sand and soil." The answer is "third eyelid" or just "eyelid".

questions.text: The idiom "to badger someone" is unrelated to the ________ of badgers.
questions.explanation: The passage states the idiom is "unrelated to their actual character." The answer is "character" — the word "actual" is an intensifier in the passage and cannot be included in the answer because it does not fit the grammar of the question sentence.

title: Sentence Completion: Water Pollution
passage: Clean and plentiful water provides the foundation for prosperous communities. We rely on clean water to survive, yet right now we are heading towards a water crisis. Changing climate patterns are threatening lakes and rivers, and key sources that we tap for drinking water are being overdrawn or tainted with pollution. NRDC experts are helping to secure safe and sufficient water for people and the environment by promoting water efficiency strategies to help decrease the amount of water wasted, protecting our water from pollution by defending the Clean Water Act and advocating for solutions like green infrastructure, helping prepare cities, counties and states for water-related challenges they will face as a result of climate change, and ensuring that waterways have enough water to support vibrant aquatic ecosystems. Dirty water is the world's biggest health risk, and continues to threaten both quality of life and public health in the United States. When water from rain and melting snow runs off roofs and roads into our rivers, it picks up toxic chemicals, dirt, trash and disease-carrying organisms along the way. Many of our water resources also lack basic protection, making them vulnerable to pollution from factory farms, industrial plants, and activities like fracking.

questions.text: The keystone to any thriving society is to have ________ and ________ water.
questions.explanation: Both words must be included as they appear together in the passage's opening: "Clean and plentiful water provides the foundation for prosperous communities." Do not include "and" as it would make the sentence grammatically incorrect.

questions.text: With the increase in water pollution a ________ is imminent.
questions.explanation: Found in the second sentence of the passage: "yet right now we are heading towards a water crisis." The word "water" is optional but recommended for specificity.

questions.text: One way to help keep water clean is by the construction of ________.
questions.explanation: Located in the passage under NRDC's work: "advocating for solutions like green infrastructure." No article should precede this answer.

questions.text: Dirty water can be a ________ as chemicals and other pollutants enter the water supply.
questions.explanation: Liz clarifies the answer cannot be "biggest health risk" because the grammar requires "a health risk," not "a biggest health risk," which is incorrect English. The word "biggest" from the passage cannot grammatically fit into the sentence.

questions.text: Due to a lack of ________, some of our water resources are at risk of pollution.
questions.explanation: The passage states many water resources "lack basic protection." Either "basic protection" or just "protection" is acceptable — "basic" is optional but not required.

title: Matching Paragraph Information: Amundsen's South Pole Expedition
passage:
A. The first expedition to reach the geographic South Pole was led by the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen. He and four others arrived at the pole on 14 December 1911, five weeks ahead of a British party led by Robert Falcon Scott as part of the Terra Nova Expedition. Amundsen and his team returned safely to their base, and later learned that Scott and his four companions had died on their return journey.

B. Amundsen's plans had focused on the Arctic and the conquest of the North Pole by means of an extended drift in an icebound ship. He obtained the use of Fridtjof Nansen's polar exploration ship Fram, and undertook extensive fundraising. Preparations for this expedition were disrupted when, in 1909, the rival American explorers Frederick Cook and Robert E. Peary each claimed to have reached the North Pole. Amundsen then changed his plan and began to prepare for a conquest of the South Pole; uncertain of the extent to which the public and his backers would support him, he kept this revised objective secret. When he set out in June 1910, even most of his crew believed they were embarking on an Arctic drift.

C. The expedition's success was widely applauded. The story of Scott's heroic failure overshadowed its achievement in the United Kingdom, unable to accept that a Norwegian had been the first person to set foot in the South Pole, but not in the rest of the world. Amundsen's decision to keep his true plans secret until the last moment was criticised by some. Recent polar historians have more fully recognised the skill and courage of Amundsen's party; the permanent scientific base at the pole bears his name, together with that of Scott.

questions.text: The success of Roald Amundsen was celebrated worldwide, except in one country.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C states: "The story of Scott's heroic failure overshadowed its achievement in the United Kingdom, unable to accept that a Norwegian had been the first person to set foot in the South Pole, but not in the rest of the world." This tells us the success was celebrated worldwide except in the UK.

questions.text: Amundsen only heard about the death of Scott after he had reached the South Pole.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A states that Amundsen and his team "returned safely to their base, and later learned that Scott and his four companions had died on their return journey." The key word is "later" — he only heard about Scott's death after the expedition.

questions.text: The base at the South Pole bears both Amundsen's name and Scott's.

questions.text: Amundsen had originally planned an expedition to the North Pole.

questions.explanation: Paragraph B states: "uncertain of the extent to which the public and his backers would support him, he kept this revised objective secret. When he set out in June 1910, even most of his crew believed they were embarking on an Arctic drift." He did not reveal his true intention to head for the South Pole.

questions.text: The British did not celebrate Amundsen's success as did other countries due to the death of Scott.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C states: "The story of Scott's heroic failure overshadowed its achievement in the United Kingdom." The British focus was on Scott's death rather than Amundsen's success, unlike the rest of the world.

title: Categorisation: Beds in the Ancient World
passage:
Bed styles in ancient Egypt remained very much the same for over 2000 years. They are among the most intriguing of furniture items because of their structure. Many were slanted down at an incline from the headboard. A footboard ensured that the sleeper would not slip off in the middle of the night. Furniture makers also constructed side rails on many beds. Almost all beds featured legs in the form of animal legs, ranging from heavy bulls legs to gazelle-like forms with hooves, and the feline type with paw and claw, frequently identified as lions legs. The mattress was usually made of wooden slats, plaited string, or reeds, which then held woollen cushions or some other soft material. Sheets were made of linen.

Roman bed-frames were pretty much the same. It would have had a mattress on top of it, stuffed with feathers or straw, and wool blankets. But most Etruscan and Roman beds would have been made of wood and strung with wool or linen string. In the bedrooms, the ceilings were vaulted and lower above the bed, often making the room appear a cramped and stuffy place.

In Ancient Greece, the beds of persons of high rank was covered with skins upon which the pillows were placed, and over these linen sheets or carpets were spread. Lastly, there was thick woollen cover or blanket for the sleeper. Poor persons slept on skins or beds of dry herbs spread upon the ground. The covers of such pillows are striped in several pictures on ancient vases and were therefore probably of various colours. They were undoubtedly filled with the same materials as the beds and mattresses.

questions.text: Bedrooms did not seem spacious.
questions.explanation: The passage about Roman bedrooms states: "the ceilings were vaulted and lower above the bed, often making the room appear a cramped and stuffy place." Cramped means not spacious, so the answer is B (Ancient Roman).

questions.text: The beds were not flat and horizontal but rather angled downwards.
questions.explanation: The passage about Ancient Egypt states: "Many were slanted down at an incline from the headboard." This means the beds were angled/inclined rather than flat and horizontal. The answer is A (Ancient Egyptian).

questions.text: Pillows could be decorative.
questions.explanation: The passage about Ancient Greece states that pillows "are striped in several pictures on ancient vases" — decorative striped pillows depicted on artwork indicates they could be decorative. The answer is C (Ancient Greek).

questions.text: Mattresses were stuffed with wool.
questions.explanation: The passage about Ancient Greece states the mattress "was filled with either wool or some other material." This is distinct from the Roman beds where the mattress was stuffed with feathers or straw (not wool). The answer is C (Ancient Greek).

title: Matching Paragraph Information: Using Online Translations for Medical Purposes
passage:
A. A complex medical and treatment discussion with patients whose knowledge of the local language is inadequate remains challenging. After treating a child whose parents did not speak English, we resorted to the use of a web based translation tool. We were unsure as to whether Google Translate was accurately translating our complex medical phrases. We aimed to evaluate the accuracy and usefulness of Google Translate in translating common English medical statements.

B. Ten commonly used medical statements were chosen by author consensus. These were translated via Google Translate to 26 languages. Translations only were sent to native speakers of each language and translated back into English by them. The returning English phrases were compared with the originals and assessed for meaning. Minor grammatical errors were accepted but not if the meaning was altered.

C. The results showed that of the ten medical phrases translated by Google Translate and then translated back into English, 57.7% were correct and 42.3% were wrong. Out of the 26 languages used, African languages scored the lowest, followed by Asian languages. Western European languages were the most accurate. However, there were some serious errors discovered. For instance, "Your child is fitting" translated in Swahili to "Your child is dead".

D. The conclusion drawn is that in today's world "just google it" is considered to be the answer to everything, but for health related questions this should be treated with caution. Google Translate should not be used for taking consent for surgery, procedures, or research from patients or relatives unless all other avenues to find human translators have been exhausted and the procedure is clinically urgent.

questions.text: It is believed that most information and help can be found on google.

questions.text: The research was conducted after a situation in which a patient's relatives did not speak English.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A states: "After treating a child whose parents did not speak English, we resorted to the use of a web based translation tool." This clinical situation — involving a patient whose relatives did not speak English — motivated the subsequent research.

questions.explanation: Paragraph D states: "Google Translate should not be used for taking consent for surgery, procedures, or research from patients or relatives unless all other avenues to find human translators have been exhausted and the procedure is clinically urgent." title: Matching Headings: Antimicrobial Resistance
passage:
Section A: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is resistance of a microorganism to an antimicrobial drug that was originally effective for treatment of infections caused by it. Resistant microorganisms are able to withstand attack by antimicrobial drugs so that standard treatments become ineffective. Resistance arises through natural evolution but the misuse and overuse of antimicrobial drugs are accelerating this process.

Section B: New mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance emerge and spread worldwide threatening our ability to treat common infectious diseases. The consequences for patients without effective treatments are catastrophic, and the problem is likely to affect people in poorer nations most severely.

Section C: The death rate for patients with serious infections caused by common bacteria treated in hospitals can be about twice that of patients with infections caused by the same non-resistant bacteria. Extended illness and treatment in intensive care units are common and result in greater economic hardship for affected families.

Section D: Resistance is happening right now, across the world, in all countries. Without urgent action, we are heading for a post-antibiotic era in which common infections and minor injuries can once again kill.

questions.text: Section A
questions.explanation: Section A defines what antimicrobial resistance is: "Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is resistance of a microorganism to an antimicrobial drug." The entire paragraph explains the concept and its causes. The correct heading is vi – What is antimicrobial resistance?

questions.text: Section B
questions.explanation: Section B states that new resistance mechanisms "spread worldwide" and that "the problem is likely to affect people in poorer nations most severely" — the focus is on the worldwide/global spread and concern. The correct heading is ii – A global concern.

questions.text: Section C
questions.explanation: Section C discusses the death rate doubling for patients with resistant infections, extended illness, and intensive care treatment. The paragraph focuses on the fatal and severe consequences of AMR. The correct heading is i – A fatal threat.

questions.text: Section D
questions.explanation: Section D describes what is happening "right now, across the world" and warns that "without urgent action, we are heading for a post-antibiotic era." The focus is on the current, present situation and its urgency. The correct heading is v – The present situation.

title: Choosing a Title: Baby Vision
passage:
Paragraph A: Babies learn to see over a period of time, much like they learn to walk and talk. They are not born with all the visual abilities they need in life. The ability to focus their eyes, move them accurately, and use them together as a team must be learned. Also, they need to learn how to use the visual information the eyes send to their brain in order to understand the world around them and interact with it appropriately.

Paragraph B: From birth, babies begin exploring the wonders of the world with their eyes. Even before they learn to reach and grab with their hands or crawl and sit-up, their eyes are providing information and stimulation important for their development. Healthy eyes and good vision play a critical role in how infants learn to see. This is why it is important that parents take this into consideration when preparing a new born baby's room. Providing interesting visual stimulus is crucial for a baby's visual development. This can include the use of colours, mobile toys and images.

Paragraph C: Research using the "visual cliff" experiment with infants ages two to three months demonstrated their ability to perceive differences between shallow and deep surfaces through heart rate variations, suggesting depth perception develops very early in life.

questions.text: Which is the best title for the reading passage above?
options: A – The importance of vision in babies
B – The role of vision to human development
C – The development of perception in babies
questions.explanation: Option C – "The development of perception in babies" – is correct. The passage takes us through details of visual development in babies and then focuses on one type of perception (depth perception), with the main paragraph about testing this development. Option A about "the importance of vision" would require content about the dangers of not developing certain vision types and why they are critical. With choosing a title questions, it is essential to pay attention to the differences in each word — the critical distinction here is between "the development of" and "the importance of". It is common to get stuck comparing "vision" and "perception" and ignore these critical difference words.

title: Multiple Choice: Alzheimer's Blood Test
passage:
The world's first blood test to predict Alzheimer's disease before symptoms occur has been developed. The test identifies 10 chemicals in the blood associated with the disease two to three years before symptoms start, but it might be able to predict Alzheimer's decades earlier.

Globally, 35 million people are living with Alzheimer's. It is characterised by a toxic build up of amyloid and tau proteins in the brain, which destroys the neurons. Several blood tests can diagnose the disease, but until now, none have had the sensitivity to predict its onset.

But with no treatments available, would anyone want to take these tests? Mapstone says "In my experience, the majority of people are very interested to know whether they will get Alzheimer's. They believe that knowledge is power – particularly when it comes to your own health. We may not have any therapy yet but there are things we can do – we can get our financial and legal affairs in order, plan for future care, and inform family members."

questions.text: The test can predict Alzheimer's…
options: A – two or three years before signs of the illness begin
B – two or three years from the start of the symptoms
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A – "before symptoms start" (= before signs of the illness begin). The passage states the test "identifies 10 chemicals... two to three years before symptoms start." It also says it "might be able to predict Alzheimer's decades earlier" — but this is only a possibility ("might"), not a confirmed capability. The question asks what the test "can" do with certainty.

questions.text: This test is the first blood test which can…
options: A – indicate possible treatments of Alzheimer's
B – estimate the start of the disease
C – offer insight into the disease
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B – "estimate the start" (= predict its onset). The passage states: "Several blood tests can diagnose the disease, but until now, none have had the sensitivity to predict its onset." The key phrase is "until now" — meaning: now this test can do it. This is the first blood test able to predict onset.

questions.text: Mapstone believes that…
options: A – this test will help people understand Alzheimer's
B – people want to know about their health
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Mapstone believes people are interested in knowing about their health. He is quoted as saying: "In my experience, the majority of people are very interested to know whether they will get Alzheimer's. They believe that knowledge is power – particularly when it comes to your own health."

title: Summary Completion: The Importance of Sleep
passage:
Sleep plays a vital role in good health and well-being throughout your life. Getting enough quality sleep at the right times can help protect your mental health, physical health, quality of life, and safety.

The way you feel while you're awake depends in part on what happens while you're sleeping. During sleep, your body is working to support healthy brain function and maintain your physical health. In children and teens, sleep also helps support growth and development.

The damage from sleep deficiency can occur in an instant (such as a car crash), or it can harm you over time. For example, ongoing sleep deficiency can raise your risk for some chronic health problems. It also can affect how well you think, react, work, learn, and get along with others.

questions.text: Physical and mental health is at risk without sufficient ________ sleep.
questions.explanation: The passage states: "Getting enough quality sleep at the right times can help protect your mental health, physical health, quality of life, and safety." The word "quality" describes the type of sleep needed — the summary refers to sufficient quality sleep.

questions.text: Furthermore, for adolescents, sleep promotes ________ and development.
questions.explanation: The passage states: "In children and teens, sleep also helps support growth and development." "Adolescents" in the summary = "children and teens" in the passage. The answer "growth" comes directly from this sentence.

questions.text: Lack of sleep can be the cause of ________ health problems which can also have an impact on important aspects of our lives.
questions.explanation: The passage states: "ongoing sleep deficiency can raise your risk for some chronic health problems." "Chronic" means long-term, continual, or unending. "Lack of sleep" in the summary = "sleep deficiency" in the passage.

title: Short Answer Questions: The History of Painted Eggs
passage:
Easter eggs, also known as Paschal eggs in some parts of the world, are special eggs often given to celebrate Easter or springtime. The practice of decorating eggshell dates back thousands of years. Ostrich eggs with engraved decoration that are 60,000 years old have been found in Africa. As far as historians know, the act of egg decoration did not have any religious origin and was just decorative. In Persian culture, eggs were sometimes painted by the whole family as they sat together preparing for the arrival of Spring and their New Year.

Eventually, eggs which often symbolised Spring become connected to the celebration of Easter. In Europe, it was traditional to use dyed and painted chicken eggs at Easter, but a modern custom is to substitute chocolate eggs, or plastic eggs filled with confectionery such as jelly beans. Easter eggs are a widely popular symbol of new life in Bulgaria, Poland, Romania, Russia, Ukraine, and other Central European countries where they are concealed in the garden for children to find.

In Russia, the incredible Peter Carl Faberge took the concept of eggs as decoration to another level. He created 50 Imperial Easter Eggs between 1885 to 1916. His remarkable eggs were made of gold, silver and other materials and were inlaid with pearls and precious gems, each egg completely unique and exquisite.

The Easter Bunny is another symbol associated with Easter. Some people believe that the Easter Bunny came about because both eggs and rabbits are often seen as symbols of fertility. Others believe the Easter Bunny originated in Germany where it judged how well behaved or not well behaved children had been by the start of the season.

questions.text: What is another name for an Easter Egg?
questions.explanation: The passage states: "Easter eggs, also known as Paschal eggs in some parts of the world" — "Paschal egg" is given directly as the alternative name. Note: brackets in the answer "(egg)" mean the word is optional.

questions.text: What type of egg was used for decoration in the ancient world?
questions.explanation: The passage states: "Ostrich eggs with engraved decoration that are 60,000 years old have been found in Africa." Ostrich eggs were used for decoration in the ancient world.

questions.text: What type of sweets were artificial eggs sometimes filled with?
questions.explanation: The passage states: "a modern custom is to substitute chocolate eggs, or plastic eggs filled with confectionery such as jelly beans." Jelly beans are the specific type of sweet mentioned.

questions.text: Where are egg hunts often conducted as part of a hide and seek game in some countries?
questions.explanation: The passage states eggs "are concealed in the garden for children to find." The answer "garden" comes directly from this sentence. Using brackets like "(garden)" in your answer key means both "garden" with or without brackets are acceptable.

questions.text: By and large, what two things did eggs represent?
questions.explanation: The passage states eggs "symbolised Spring" in general, and later notes eggs represent "fertility and rebirth." Both words are required — do not use "and" between them, just write the two words. Using a comma would not be counted wrong.

questions.text: What determined if children had been naughty or nice at the beginning of Spring?
questions.explanation: The passage states: "it was the Easter Bunny who would determine who had been naughty or nice at the beginning of Spring." The Easter Bunny made this determination.

title: Matching Sentence Endings: Crime and Punishment
passage:
Debates over how to treat prisoners have gone on since imprisonment began: should the prison system leave inmates to fester in cold cells, with punishment and deterrence as the goal of incarceration? Or should it let them wander from classroom to games room, preaching rehabilitation into society as its main aim?

With over 83,000 prisoners currently locked away, England and Wales have a staggering imprisonment rate of 150 per 100,000 of the population. Our prisons have been officially overcrowded since 1994; nearly 14,000 current inmates are serving indeterminate sentences. If lowering the number of criminals is the reason behind imprisonment, recent figures point to a failing system: almost three quarters of under-18s are reconvicted within a year of release. As James Bell, an American lawyer and prison reform activist, said: "As it stands now, justice systems are extremely expensive, do not rehabilitate, but in fact make the people that experience them worse."

In response to worldwide alarm over the ineffectiveness of how we manage criminals, a growing number of prisons are embracing a new style of incarceration. By giving inmates more responsibility, comfort, and freedom within the prison walls, governors say they are offering prisoners the chance to change. As the Prison Radio Association spokespeople said: "Reducing re-offending is of benefit to everybody. Equipping prisoners with skills and confidence is crucial in bringing down re-offending rates."

title: Sentence Completion: The War on Smoking
passage:
Make no mistake, the move to introduce plain packaging is just the latest front in the war against smoking. Over the past decade, there has been a ban on smoking in public places and moves to restrict displays in shops. But one of the issues that has been concerning health experts and ministers is the number of people who continue to take up smoking, particularly young people.

More than 200,000 under-16s start smoking in the UK each year — helping ensure a viable market remains for manufacturers once the number of people quitting and dying is taken into account. In countries like the UK where there is a ban on advertising, the pack remains the last major vehicle for promotion. Hence the detail and care taken in the design of the packets with their laminated and special print effects, foil decorations and slide openings and bevelled edges. It should come as no surprise therefore to learn that they have become known as the "silent salesman" and "mobile billboard" within the industry.

questions.text: __________ is the most recent strategy to tackle the problem of smoking.
questions.explanation: The passage states "the move to introduce plain packaging is just the latest front in the war against smoking" — "latest" = most recent strategy. The answer is "plain packaging".

questions.text: The large number of new smokers, particularly under 16s, makes certain that cigarette companies will always have a __________.
questions.explanation: The passage refers to new smokers (particularly under 16s) as what makes cigarette companies a "viable market." The word "viable" means workable/profitable — it adds value to the sentence. Either "viable market" or just "market" is acceptable.

questions.text: In some countries, packaging is the only method that cigarette companies have for __________.
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states: "the pack remains the last major vehicle for promotion." The exact word from the passage is "promotion" — not "advertising," which is a synonym but not the word used in the passage. In sentence completion, you must use the exact word from the text.

questions.text: Packets are seen as being the __________ in the cigarette industry.
questions.explanation: The passage refers to cigarette packets as both "the silent salesman" and "mobile billboard." You should choose only one answer — writing both would be incorrect under IELTS rules.

title: Summary Completion: Fermented Foods
passage:
Fermentation is a process in which an agent (typically bacteria and yeast) cause an organic substance to break down into simpler substances; especially, the anaerobic breakdown of sugar into alcohol. It is used to produce alcoholic beverages and preserve foods like sauerkraut, kimchi, and yogurt.

Dr. Elie Metchnikoff, a Nobel Prize winner, recognised fermented food benefits in the early 1900s. He believed the daily ingestion of yogurt was a major contribution to the superior health and longevity of Bulgarians. Bulgarians developed techniques for detoxifying and preserving milk, converting it into yogurt and cheese. In Europe, wine was consumed as clean water; Caucasians used Kefir grains similarly. Various vegetables were fermented for preservation in different countries — kimchi in Korea, sauerkraut in Germany. However, the fermentation process was too lengthy and not uniform so for wide scale food production manufacturers turned to pickling instead.

questions.text: At the start of the 20th century, Dr. Metchnikoff put forward his belief that the ________ and good health of Bulgarians could be attributed to eating fermented food each day.
questions.explanation: The passage states Dr. Metchnikoff "believed the daily ingestion of yogurt was a major contribution to the superior health and longevity of Bulgarians." "Longevity" = long life/lifespan, and it is the answer from the word list (option C).

questions.text: By ________ and preserving milk, they were able to convert it into yogurt and cheese.
questions.explanation: The passage states "Bulgarians developed techniques for detoxifying and preserving milk, converting it into yogurt and cheese." "Detoxifying" (option I) fills the blank — the process of removing harmful substances from milk before preserving it.

questions.text: They were able to convert milk into ________ and cheese.
questions.explanation: The passage states Bulgarians converted milk "into yogurt and cheese." "Yogurt" (option B) is the first product mentioned.

questions.text: They were able to convert milk into yogurt and ________.
questions.explanation: The passage states Bulgarians converted milk "into yogurt and cheese." "Cheese" (option H) is the second product mentioned.

questions.text: In other parts of Europe, fermented ________ was consumed as a replacement for clean water.
questions.explanation: The passage states "In Europe, wine was consumed as clean water." Wine (option E) was the fermented drink used as a replacement for clean water.

questions.text: People used to ferment ________ which gave them a longer lifespan but nowadays mass production favours pickling.
questions.explanation: The passage states "Various vegetables were fermented for preservation in different countries." The answer is "vegetables" (option J). title: Matching Paragraph Information: Hobbies for the Elderly
passage:
A. Card Making: This has become an increasingly popular hobby, as it's very easy to start and cards can be as simple or complicated as skills allow. Designs can be from templates or completely unique to the person making them. Best of all, it's a beautiful form of communication with an added personal touch. All family members will relish receiving these personalised cards from someone they love.

B. Art: This can be done at your parent's home, or in a local art class. It can be painting, drawing, sculpture, or pottery. It does not matter how skilled your parent is, as there are opportunities for all levels. Just give it a go. The creative process is very absorbing and rewarding and it is a great way for your elderly relative to meet new people.

C. Getting Online: If your aging parent likes the look of new technology, but has never learned how to use it, the internet is very easy once someone has shown them how. It opens up a whole new world of information and they will be able to keep in touch easily with children and grandchildren via email, apps, groups and many more exciting options.

D. Playing Cards: What a great way to socialise and have fun at the same time. Playing cards helps keep your brain sharp by remembering strategies and keeping up the cards already played. These games are played in a group and your parent will be paired with another player. This is a great way to form lasting bonds with other elderly people.

E. Dance: This is a great way to spend an afternoon or evening. The dance sessions are run by a professional dancer who also have experience in teaching elderly people. This is a chance for them to experience dances from their youth with other likeminded people. And it's never too late to bring a bit of spice and romance into someone's life through dance.

questions.text: Offering new methods of communication.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C states the internet lets elderly people "keep in touch easily with children and grandchildren via email, apps, groups and many more exciting options." This refers to new methods of communication.

questions.text: It's good to bring the past to life.

questions.text: Keeping mentally astute helps elderly people.

questions.text: Tapping into one's inventiveness through various forms.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B states art "can be painting, drawing, sculpture, or pottery" — various forms of creative art. "Tapping into one's inventiveness through various forms" matches this description of the creative process across multiple art forms.

title: Matching Sentence Endings: NASA Orion
passage:
A US space capsule that could help get humans to Mars is about to make its maiden flight. Orion will be launched on a Delta rocket out of Cape Canaveral in Florida on a short journey above the Earth to test key technologies. The conical vessel is reminiscent of the Apollo command ships that took men to the Moon in the 1960s and 1970s, but bigger and with cutting-edge systems. Given that this is a first outing, there will be no people aboard.

Nonetheless, the US space agency describes the demonstration as a major event. Nasa has a window in which to launch Orion of about two-and-a-half hours, which began at 07:05 local time (12:05 GMT). The launch preparations had to be stopped shortly before the opening of the window because a boat strayed into the eastern part of the launch range. After that, the countdown had to be held because of strong winds and a technical issue.

Orion is being developed alongside a powerful new rocket that will have its own debut in the near future. Together, they will form the core capabilities needed to send humans beyond the International Space Station to destinations such as the Red Planet. For Thursday's flight, the Delta IV-Heavy rocket – currently the beefiest launcher in the world – is being used as a stand-in. It will send Orion twice around the globe, throwing the ship up to an altitude of almost 6,000km. This will set up a fast fall back to Earth, with a re-entry speed into the atmosphere close to 30,000km/h – near what would be expected of a capsule coming back from the Moon. It should give engineers the opportunity to check the performance of Orion's critical heat shield, which is likely to experience temperatures in excess of 2,000°C.
