title: Matching Headings: Pangolins
passage:
Paragraph A: Pangolins, often called 'scaly anteaters,' are covered in tough, overlapping scales. These burrowing mammals eat ants and termites using an extraordinarily long, sticky tongue, and are able to quickly roll themselves up into a tight ball when threatened. Eight different pangolin species can be found across Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Poaching for illegal wildlife trade and habitat loss have made these incredible creatures one of the most endangered groups of mammals in the world.

Paragraph B: There are detailed physical descriptions of pangolins including size variations, coloration, scale composition (keratin), tongue characteristics, and sensory adaptations.

Paragraph C: There are eight pangolin species. All pangolins belong to the genus Manis in the family Manidae, which is the only family within the order Pholidota. Pangolins' closest living relatives are the Xenarthrans – anteaters, armadillos, and sloths.

Paragraph D: Pangolins are found in a range of habitats across Africa and Asia, from tropical forests to dry woodlands. They use burrows for shelter and raising young.

Paragraph E: Pangolins are nocturnal. They sleep during the day, curled up into a ball or in their burrows. When threatened, they curl up tightly and use their sharp-scaled tail as a defensive weapon.

Paragraph F: Pangolins feed almost exclusively on ants and termites. Their long, sticky tongues can extend beyond the length of their bodies to lap up insects. In captivity, their highly specialised diet makes them very difficult to care for.

Paragraph G: Pangolins are among the most trafficked mammals in the world. They are hunted for their scales, which are used in traditional medicine, and for their meat. International trade in pangolins is banned, but illegal poaching continues to threaten all eight species.

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.explanation: Paragraph A introduces pangolins for the first time, describing what they are: scaly anteaters covered in tough overlapping scales that eat ants. This introductory overview matches heading viii – What is a pangolin?

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.explanation: Paragraph B provides detailed physical descriptions: size variations, coloration, scale composition, tongue characteristics, and sensory adaptations. This is a description of the animal's physical features, matching heading ix – Description of a pangolin.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.explanation: Paragraph C discusses the 8 species, the genus Manis, the family Manidae, the order Pholidota, and pangolins' closest living relatives. This is about scientific classification — taxonomy. There are only two possible headings: IV Taxonomy or VII Comparison of pangolin species. The paragraph does not compare the 8 species (no sizes, diets or habitats are contrasted) — its aim is purely classification. Therefore heading iv – Taxonomy is correct.

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.explanation: Paragraph D describes where pangolins are found: across Africa and Asia, in tropical forests to dry woodlands, using burrows for shelter. This matches heading ii – Distribution and habitat.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes pangolin behaviour: nocturnal habits, sleeping curled up, defensive response when threatened. This matches heading iii – Pangolin behaviour.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.explanation: Paragraph F is entirely about what pangolins eat: almost exclusively ants and termites, using their long sticky tongues. This matches heading xi – The pangolin diet.

questions.text: Paragraph G
questions.explanation: Paragraph G explains that pangolins are among the most trafficked mammals: hunted for scales used in traditional medicine and for their meat, despite an international trade ban. This explains why they are endangered, matching heading x – Why pangolins are endangered.

title: Matching Headings: Desertification — Causes and Effects
passage:
Causes of Desertification

Paragraph A: Trees are being cut down at much larger scale than ever before to be used as fuel, to provide products we use in our daily life, or to simply create more space for agriculture to sustain growing human population. Once the trees and other vegetation in an area are gone, there is nothing left to hold the soil in place.

Paragraph B: Our planet's ecosystems sustain life only when balanced. They can cope with incremental challenges and adapt but beyond a certain tipping point they collapse. A rapid increase in the number of people demands higher amounts of natural resources and expands more and more over the landscape, leading to increased desertification.

Paragraph C: Improper irrigation methods used in arid areas, such as canal irrigation, lead to a buildup of salt in the soil and make it difficult for crops and other plants to grow, increasing desertification. Similarly harmful is cultivation of already deteriorated lands. Through inconsiderate farming methods, farmers only speed up the process of desertification in exchange for poor quality crops with low economic value.

Paragraph D: In arid regions, grass and other vegetation is necessary to keep the soil in place. If such vegetation is used as feed for cattle without sustainable control, there is nothing that remains to prevent soil from blowing or washing away, and if this process occurs long enough, it can lead to desertification.

Effects of Desertification

Paragraph E: As desertification occurs, the soil can be blown or washed away, and valuable soil nutrients are lost. As the soil dries out, it hardens and it becomes difficult for any rainfall that does occur to penetrate below the soil's surface. And what remains left is a lifeless pile of dust instead of a life-giving medium.

Paragraph F: Due to drought conditions and a loss of productive land, local people find themselves and their livestock experiencing starvation.

Paragraph G: Desertification events have been a major driver behind the movement of large human populations throughout history. When soils are not able to support their civilisation, people set on the move to look for better locations.

Paragraph H: Species that once lived in a fertile and productive climate may not survive in a newly desertified region.

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph A: "Trees are being cut down." Cutting down trees = deforestation. The correct heading is VII – Deforestation.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph B: "A rapid increase in the number of people." A rapid increase in population = overpopulation. The correct heading is III – Overpopulation.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph C: "Improper irrigation methods / inconsiderate farming methods." These are unsustainable agriculture techniques. The correct heading is IX – Unsustainable agriculture techniques.

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph D: "Feed for cattle without sustainable control." Allowing cattle to eat land without sustainable management = overgrazing. The correct heading is I – Overgrazing.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph E: "Valuable soil nutrients are lost / soil dries out / lifeless pile of dust." Loss of soil nutrients and drying out = soil infertility. The correct heading is X – Soil infertility.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph F: "People find themselves and their livestock experiencing starvation." Starvation = famine. The correct heading is V – Famine.

questions.text: Paragraph G
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph G: "Movement of large human populations." Large-scale movement of people = mass migration. The correct heading is II – Mass migration.

questions.text: Paragraph H
questions.explanation: Key words in Paragraph H: "Species … may not survive." Species that may not survive = species facing extinction. The correct heading is VI – Extinction of species.

title: Choosing a Title: Coffee
passage: Coffee is one of the most popular hot drinks in the world. Almost a third of the world's population drinks coffee. People often meet at cafes or coffee shops for a coffee break during the middle of the morning or stop work in the afternoon to drink coffee. About 7 million tons of coffee is produced every year. Brazil is, by far, the world's largest coffee producer. About a third of the world's production comes from this South American country. Other coffee producing countries include Vietnam, Indonesia and Colombia. The United States is the biggest coffee consumer in the world. About 1.2 billion kilograms of coffee are consumed there every year. Drinking coffee is extremely popular in European countries, like Italy, France and Germany, as well as in Brazil.

questions.text: Which is the best title for the passage above?
options: A – Coffee: a popular hot drink
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A – "Coffee – a popular hot drink." The opening paragraph and closing line both stress the same point: the popularity of coffee. When both the opening and closing of a passage stress the same point with so much detail, that is the main aim. There are no fixed rules, but you must ask yourself: Why did the author write this passage? What was the key message? In this case, information about producers and consumers is extra detail given for interest — but the main aim was to explain the popularity of coffee.

title: Sentence Completion: Life on Earth
passage:
Life on Earth started around 3.8 billion years ago and has since evolved and diversified through the process of natural selection to be adapted to almost every environment possible. There are currently an estimated 1.9 million animals, plants, and other forms of life on Earth.

Life can be found in every nook and cranny of the globe, from the extreme environments of deep sea hydrothermal vents and the freezing conditions of the Polar Regions to the lush habitats found at the equator.

Looking back through time, by means of the fossil and phylogenetic record, we can see that the Earth has been home to many more species than are alive today. Taking a historical perspective shows that life is constantly evolving, with the success and dominance of different groups waxing and waning over time.

The diversity of life is truly amazing, but all living organisms do share certain similarities. All living organisms can replicate, and the replicator molecule is DNA. As well, all living organisms contain some means of converting the information stored in DNA into products used to build cellular machinery from fats, proteins, and carbohydrates.

questions.text: The world has been developed and changed by ________ for over 3.8 billion years.
questions.explanation: "Developed and changed" = evolved and diversified. The answer is "natural selection." Note: it is not possible to say "the natural selection" (no article) or "natural selection process" (adds a word not in the passage).

questions.text: The past history of the species that used to exist on earth can be found through the ________ record.
questions.explanation: "Past history of species" = looking back through time using the fossil and phylogenetic record. Both words are required and spelling must be correct.

questions.text: The coming and going of specific groups and species can illustrate to us that life is forever ________.
questions.explanation: "Coming and going" = waxing and waning. "Forever" = constantly. The answer is "evolving" — life is constantly/forever in a state of evolving.

questions.text: Without ________, life forms would not be able to replicate.
questions.explanation: "Life forms" = living organisms. DNA is what allows living organisms to replicate. Without DNA, life forms would not be able to replicate.

title: Paraphrasing / Summary Completion: Egyptian Blue
passage: Crime scene investigators are about to get an assist from the land of the pharaohs. New research has shown that a pigment called Egyptian blue, formulated some 5,250 years ago, can be used as dusting powder to detect fingerprints on complicated surfaces. The earliest known synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue is found in some of the paint that still colours ancient statues, coffins, and tomb walls. Modern scientists were intrigued by this long-lasting tint and figured out its chemical components decades ago. More recently they discovered that it emits near-infrared radiation when exposed to a certain kind of light.

questions.text: The pigment ________ Egyptian blue, which was formulated about 5,250 years ago, can now be used to identify fingerprints on complicated surfaces.
questions.explanation: "Known as" is the correct paraphrase for "called." You cannot choose "names" because it is grammatically wrong in this context.

questions.text: ...which was formulated ________ 5,250 years ago...
questions.explanation: "About" is the correct paraphrase for "some" (as in approximately). You cannot use "over" because we do not know if the figure is over or under 5,250 years — "about" is the accurate neutral paraphrase meaning approximately.

questions.text: ...can now be used to ________ fingerprints on complicated surfaces.
questions.explanation: "Identify" is the correct paraphrase for "detect." The passage says the pigment "can be used as dusting powder to detect fingerprints" — detect = identify in this context.

questions.text: ...it has now been ________ that, when it is exposed to a particular light, it emits near-infrared radiation.
questions.explanation: "Revealed" or "found" are both acceptable paraphrases for "discovered." Both words mean the same thing in this context and are grammatically correct.

questions.text: ...when it is exposed to a ________ light, it emits near-infrared radiation.
questions.explanation: "Particular" is the correct paraphrase for "certain" (as in a certain/particular kind of light). Spelling must be correct — a wrong spelling will be marked wrong.

title: Paraphrasing / Synonyms: Canaries in Coal Mines

New electronic detectors will replace the bird because they are said to be cheaper in the long run and more effective in indicating the presence of pollutants in the air otherwise unnoticed by miners. The gas detectors will be hand-held and carry a digital reading which appears on a screen alerting miners to the extent of the gases.

questions.explanation: The passage uses "phased out" as the paraphrase for "gradually stop using": "More than 200 canary birds are being phased out of Britain's mining pits." Phased out = gradually stop using.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: substitute
questions.explanation: The passage uses "replace" as the paraphrase for "substitute": "New electronic detectors will replace the bird." Replace = substitute.

questions.explanation: The passage uses "long-serving" as the paraphrase for "employed since way back": "the long-serving yellow feathered friend of the miner." Long-serving = has been employed/used for a long time.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: existence
questions.explanation: The passage uses "presence" as the paraphrase for "existence": "indicating the presence of pollutants in the air." Presence = existence.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: portable
questions.explanation: The passage uses "hand-held" as the paraphrase for "portable": "The gas detectors will be hand-held." Hand-held = portable (can be carried and used by hand).

questions.explanation: The passage uses "yellow feathered friend" as a descriptive phrase referring to the canary bird: "the long-serving yellow feathered friend of the miner." This is a paraphrase/description that avoids repeating the word "canary."

questions.text: Find a phrase in the passage that means: ultimately / in the end
questions.explanation: The passage uses "in the long run" as the paraphrase for "ultimately / in the end": "they are said to be cheaper in the long run." In the long run = ultimately.

title: Synonym Practice: Did Birds Evolve from Dinosaurs?
passage: Evidence that birds evolved from dinosaurs, the carnivorous predators that ruled the Mesozoic ecosystems is plentiful. Traditionally, the prime source of evidence in support of this scientific view was the similar shape of the bones of birds but spectacular new discoveries have added other lines of evidence to the table. One of these involves a suite of features from the eggs of these dinosaurs. A host of fossils have shown that not only did maniraptoran dinosaurs resemble birds in the way they laid their eggs but that these eggs also looked like the eggs of birds. Another line of evidence involves fossils of animals in a brooding pose or in resting postures also show a startling similarity with the behaviours we see among living birds. Yet, perhaps the most compelling new line of evidence comes from the discovery of soft tissues associated with the skeletons of these predatory dinosaurs, many fossils of these creatures are now known to have been covered by plumage. All this evidence has highlighted the fact that many features that were previously thought to be exclusively avian — from feathers to a wishbone — have now been discovered in the immediate dinosaur predecessor of birds. Even flight is likely to have been an attribute inherited by birds from their dinosaurian forebears.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: meat-eating
questions.explanation: The passage uses "carnivorous" as the synonym for meat-eating: "the carnivorous predators that ruled the Mesozoic ecosystems." Carnivorous = meat-eating.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: a group or set
questions.explanation: The passage uses "suite" as the synonym for a group or set: "a suite of features from the eggs of these dinosaurs." Suite = a group/set of related things.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: stance or position
questions.explanation: The passage uses "pose" as the synonym for stance or position: referring to the posture/stance of the dinosaurs. Pose = stance or position.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: resemblance
questions.explanation: The passage uses "similarity" as the synonym for resemblance: describing how dinosaurs and birds share similar features. Similarity = resemblance.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: persuasive / most convincing
questions.explanation: The passage uses "compelling" as the synonym for persuasive or convincing: referring to the most persuasive/convincing evidence. Compelling = persuasive.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: feathers
questions.explanation: The passage uses "plumage" as the synonym for feathers. This was the most difficult word — if you are aiming for band 7 or above, you should have known this vocabulary. Plumage = feathers.

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: ancestor
questions.explanation: The passage uses "forebears" as the synonym for ancestor. Note: "predecessor" is another possible answer in terms of meaning but it appears at a different point in the passage than "forebears."

questions.text: Find a word in the passage that means: characteristic or quality
questions.explanation: The passage uses "attribute" as the synonym for characteristic or quality. Note: "features" is another possible answer in terms of meaning but it appears before "forebears/predecessor" in the passage.
